title: Advice to avoid confrontational tone
description: This latent fires on imperative-style advice instructing the reader to avoid aggressive, accusatory, defensive, or interrupting behavior during a conversation, typically phrased as 'Avoid X or Y' or 'Speak calmly/firmly...' directives about tone and demeanor. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic bullet-point style admonitions (often bolded headers like 'Stay calm and assertive**:') that prescribe communication conduct—avoiding raised voices, blame, sarcasm, or dominating the conversation—rather than on advice about the content or substance of what to say. It does not activate strongly on sentences that merely describe a situation, analyze someone's behavior, offer sympathy, or give advice unrelated to tone/demeanor (e.g., apologizing, reframing complaints, or general relationship tips), even though these appear in similar advice-giving contexts. The key distinguishing feature is the explicit prescriptive framing around vocal/emotional tone and interpersonal comportment ('avoid being confrontational', 'speak calmly'), not just general conflict-resolution advice.

title: Conversational request/proposal openers
description: This latent fires on short, direct interpersonal utterances that propose, request, or check in on something in a conversation — especially modal-verb question openers like 'Can we...', 'Can you...', 'Would you...', and short check-in phrases like 'Is everything okay?' or 'I wanted to reach out.' It activates most strongly on these quoted, ready-to-say conversational lines themselves (often suggested scripts for talking to someone, changing topics, catching up, or asking permission), rather than on descriptions or analysis of a conversation. It does not activate on third-person explanatory or advice-giving prose that discusses what someone should say or how they feel (e.g. 'You could explain that...', 'She might have felt...'), even when topically similar, since the latent responds to the direct first/second-person spoken request form rather than meta-commentary about communication.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the standalone numeral (and following punctuation) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '3.' or '4.' at the start of a line, typically within reasoning that lays out points, reasons, or considerations. It activates most strongly on bare list markers isolated from surrounding text, and more weakly on sentences that are themselves list items introducing a claim (e.g. 'Here's why: 1.' or numbered bolded headers like '2. **'). It does not activate on prose sentences that lack an explicit list-numbering token, even if they discuss similar reasoning or perspective-taking content, nor on list markers using bullets or letters instead of arabic numerals.

title: Suggested-activity list items
description: This latent fires on list-style suggestions of activities, hobbies, or events to try or join—typically phrased as 'Attend/Join/Take X, Y, or Z' or 'This could be a concert, a book club, or...'. It activates most strongly on bullet points or sentences enumerating leisure, social, or self-improvement options (concerts, festivals, classes, clubs, sports teams, museums, side-hustle ideas) often within advice-giving lists recommending ways to meet people, find hobbies, or earn money. It does not activate on general advice, emotional support, or relationship guidance that lacks this enumerative 'try one of these activities/options' structure, nor on narrative or reflective sentences even if they mention similar topics (e.g. a sentence just praising music or discussing feelings about hobbies without listing concrete activity options).

title: Partial hedged agreement/disagreement
description: This latent fires on short qualifying phrases like 'Not entirely,' 'Not necessarily,' or 'No, I don't think so' that partially affirm or deny a claim while hedging against a full yes/no answer. It activates most strongly on standalone hedge tokens of this kind, and more weakly on longer sentences that embed the same hedging move (e.g., 'you're not entirely in the wrong,' 'not necessarily about being right or wrong'), often in the context of judging someone's behavior (AITA-style responses). It would not activate on unqualified, absolute statements ('Yes,' 'No,' 'You are the asshole') or on sentences that make claims without a partial/hedging qualifier, even if they discuss the same topic of moral judgment or blame.

title: Re-evaluation prompt
description: This latent fires on short imperative or metacognitive cues that signal a pause to reconsider, review, or revise prior work or reasoning, exemplified by the standalone instruction 'Re-evaluate'. It activates on sentences functioning as directives or self-checks that prompt a reassessment step, often appearing as headers, instructions, or transitional markers in reasoning chains. It would not activate on sentences that merely describe past evaluation, state conclusions, or discuss a topic without invoking an explicit call to reconsider or redo an assessment.

title: Reframing the situation under consideration
description: This latent activates on sentences that explicitly restate or reframe the situation the reader/speaker is currently deliberating about, often using a meta-phrase like "you're now considering whether..." to name the question at hand before evaluating it. It fires on constructions that pause to name the exact dilemma, decision, or self-justification being weighed, frequently incorporating a vivid idiom or figurative phrase (e.g., "threw under the bus") to characterize the action in question. It would not activate on a simple factual statement, a direct answer to a question, or a description of an event without the framing move of stepping back to identify "what you're now weighing/considering." Sentences that merely narrate events or give conclusions without this explicit reflective framing would not trigger it.

title: Enthusiastic validating exclamation
description: This latent fires most strongly on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that affirm or celebrate something the interlocutor just said, such as 'That's wonderful!', 'That's great to hear!', 'That's exciting!', or 'That's a wonderful idea!'. At lower activation it extends to broader empathetic/validating openers that acknowledge or affirm the user's feelings or situation ('It's understandable that...', 'I totally understand!', 'You're not alone in feeling this way'), which serve a similar conversational function of emotional validation before elaborating. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, substantive advice, or critical/disagreeing responses; the key trigger is a brief affective validation move, most intensely when phrased as a punchy 'That's [positive adjective]!' exclamation rather than a longer explanatory empathy statement.

title: Validating self-prioritization ('you deserve to prioritize yourself')
description: This latent fires on reassuring, second-person statements that affirm the reader's right or entitlement to prioritize their own needs, well-being, happiness, or boundaries, typically using formulas like 'You deserve to...', 'You have the right to...', or 'It's okay to prioritize...'. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic affirmations built directly around the core verb 'prioritize' paired with 'deserve'/'right'/'okay' framing self-care as legitimate or owed. It activates more weakly on related therapeutic advice sentences that discuss boundaries, self-care, or emotional well-being in a broader advice-giving context but lack the tight 'deserve/right to prioritize' construction. It would not activate on sentences merely describing a situation, giving practical suggestions unrelated to self-worth (e.g., logistical advice), or validating a person's feelings/actions in other domains (e.g., 'you're not the asshole') without the explicit self-prioritization entitlement framing.

title: Naming harmful relational behavior and its emotional fallout
description: This latent fires on generic, evaluative sentences that label a behavior as unacceptable, toxic, abusive, or hurtful and/or enumerate the negative emotional consequences (resentment, anxiety, depression, shame, frustration) that follow from it. The pattern is a templatic assertion of the form 'This/That [behavior] is/can be [negative adjective]' or 'This can lead to feelings of [X, Y, and Z]', typically appearing as a summarizing or diagnostic statement in advice-giving text about interpersonal conflict, abuse, or discrimination. It does not activate on sentences that merely describe a situation, give advice or suggestions, express empathy/validation toward the person ('it's understandable that...'), or narrate specific events without pronouncing a general judgment or listing emotional consequences—i.e., concrete narrative detail, question-asking, and advice-oriented phrasing are excluded even when the topic is similar (toxic relationships, conflict, etc.).

title: Generic affirming statements about emotional wellbeing
description: This latent fires on templated, generalized declarative sentences that affirm or validate a psychological or emotional truth—often of the form '[X quality/state] can be [empowering/tough/valuable/isolating]' or 'It's normal/common to feel [X]'. These are abstract, aphorism-like statements about confidence, self-awareness, connection, motivation, or emotional struggle, typically delivered as a general truism rather than addressing a specific person's situation. It does NOT activate on concrete, situation-specific advice, questions, or narrative descriptions of a particular person's circumstances (e.g., 'Your mom didn't understand the elk...' or 'Are you trying to fill an awkward silence?'), nor on list items, meta-commentary, or numbered/bulleted suggestions—these instead belong to the 'random' (non-top-activating) examples, showing the latent is tuned specifically to the generic validating-statement template rather than to emotional topics broadly.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins an item in an enumerated or numbered list (e.g., '5.', '7.', '9.'), typically at the start of a line followed by a period and often bolding or a colon. It activates most strongly on bare list-number tokens themselves, and also fires (more weakly) on numbered items that introduce a bolded heading or label like '**Activities:**' or '**Step 10:**'. It does not activate on numbers that are part of ordinary prose, dates, quantities, or arithmetic expressions, nor on list markers using bullets, letters, or roman numerals instead of arabic numerals followed by a period.

title: Transitional list-preamble phrase
description: This latent fires on the short introductory phrase that precedes an enumerated list of advice, points, or reasons—e.g. 'Here are some points to consider:', 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Here's why:'—typically followed by a numbered '1.' item. It activates most strongly on the canonical templated openers (points/thoughts/suggestions 'to consider' or 'to ponder') immediately preceding the start of a numbered list, and more weakly on similar but less formulaic transition sentences that also lead into advice or breakdowns ('Let's break it down:', 'Now, let's address the issues:'). It does not activate on the substantive content of the list items themselves, nor on declarative or evaluative sentences that don't function as a lead-in to an itemized list (e.g. opinions, judgments, or narrative descriptions like 'You're not the asshole').

title: Contrastive acknowledgment before pivoting
description: This latent fires on discourse markers and phrases that acknowledge or validate a prior point (a concern, worry, or claim) before introducing a qualification or counterpoint, such as 'However,' or 'Regarding your concerns about X, it's true/valid that...'. It activates on sentence-initial or clause-initial constructions that signal an empathetic concession or transition, often in advice-giving or conversational contexts where the speaker validates the interlocutor's stated worry before adding nuance. It would not activate on simple statements of fact, direct advice without acknowledgment, or contrastive words used mid-argument without referencing a specific prior concern being validated.

title: Age-old dilemma/debate exclamation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that frame an upcoming topic as a familiar, timeless tension or unresolved question, typically of the form 'The age-old [dilemma/debate/struggle/conundrum]!' or 'The eternal [dilemma/struggle/conundrum]!'. It activates most strongly on the bare stock phrase itself (often repeated verbatim), and more weakly when the phrase is extended with a specific topic clause (e.g., 'The age-old conundrum of navigating complex friendships!'), suggesting the core trigger is the rhetorical template rather than the topic content. It does not activate on other empathetic or situational openers that lack this 'age-old/eternal + noun of tension + exclamation' framing, such as 'What a complex situation!', 'NTA', 'Let's break it down', or direct advice/analysis sentences, even though these appear in similar advice-column contexts.

title: Recommending professional/social support-seeking
description: This latent fires on stock advice-giving phrases that direct a reader to seek emotional or professional support, typically as a formulaic imperative like 'Seek support,' 'Consider seeking support from a therapist,' or 'Talk to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor.' It activates most strongly on the templated header/bullet form of this recommendation (often bolded as 'Seek support**:') found in advice-style responses, especially ones listing therapists, counselors, support groups, or trusted friends/family as resources. It is less about general supportive or empathetic language and more specifically about the recurring boilerplate suggestion to consult outside help; sentences that merely describe supportive behavior, offer other unrelated advice, or discuss support in a narrative/reflective way (rather than issuing the 'seek help/support' recommendation itself) activate it weakly or not at all.

title: Direct introspective probing questions
description: This latent fires on short, direct questions addressed to the reader/interlocutor asking them to introspect and articulate their own goals, feelings, values, priorities, or concerns (e.g., 'What are your goals?', 'What's driving you?', 'Is there something specific that's making you hesitant?'). It activates most strongly on standalone or near-standalone question sentences in this second-person, therapist/coach-style register, especially ones beginning with 'What are...', 'What's...', or 'Is there something/anything specific...'. It is weaker but still active on similar questions embedded within longer advice or reflection passages. It does NOT activate (or activates much less) on declarative advice statements, third-person questions about someone else's behavior, imperative suggestions ('Take a step back', 'Set clear boundaries'), or narrative/explanatory sentences that describe a situation rather than posing a direct introspective question to the reader.

title: Assistant helpfulness/support opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic assistant phrases that declare readiness to help, listen, or support the user, especially the canonical openers 'I'm here to help!' and 'I'm happy to help!'. It activates most strongly on these near-identical stock phrases used as conversational openers or closers, and more weakly on related but longer variants that still center on offering assistance/support/listening (e.g., 'I'm here to listen and offer support', 'I'm here to help you navigate this situation'). It does not activate strongly on substantive empathetic statements that acknowledge the user's specific feelings or situation (e.g., 'I'm so sorry to hear that...'), clarifying questions ('Can you tell me more about...'), or advice/analysis content, which express engagement but not this generic 'ready-to-assist' formula.

title: Formulaic closing advice about relationships
description: This latent fires on the stock closing-statement pattern used in relationship/interpersonal advice text, typically beginning with 'Remember,' (or 'Ultimately,'/'Remember that') and asserting that communication, compromise, empathy, respect, or understanding are 'key' or 'essential' in relationships. It activates most strongly on the near-templatic full phrase (e.g., 'Remember, communication and compromise are key in any relationship') and activates more weakly, but still fires, on related sentences that give similar summary advice or invoke communication/respect/compromise as important relational values even without the exact template. It does not activate on sentences that discuss specific situational details, judgments (e.g., 'you're the asshole'), or advice about boundaries/self-care that lack this generic 'key ingredient of relationships' framing, nor on sentences merely mentioning communication or respect as one clause among concrete situational reasoning rather than as a capstone maxim.

title: Reframing a request or reaction as reasonable
description: This latent activates on sentences that clarify or reframe an interpersonal request, boundary, or emotional reaction by explicitly negating a more extreme or unreasonable interpretation ('not asking for X', 'not surprising that...'), typically in the context of validating someone's stance in an advice-style dialogue. It fires on statements that use a 'not X, but Y' or 'not surprising' construction to reassure the reader that their expectation, feeling, or request is legitimate and within reasonable bounds. It would not activate on plain descriptive statements, straightforward advice without this negation/validation structure, or emotional reactions stated without the qualifying contrast that positions the situation as reasonable versus excessive.

title: Imperative empathetic-listening advice
description: This latent fires on short imperative directives instructing the reader to listen to, acknowledge, or validate another person's feelings, perspective, or experiences (e.g., 'Acknowledge her feelings and validate her experiences,' 'Listen to their perspective and validate their emotions'). It activates most strongly on terse, formulaic advice-list items built from a small set of verbs (acknowledge, validate, listen, understand, show empathy) paired with a possessive pronoun and an emotion/perspective noun, typically appearing as bullet-style relationship or conflict-resolution advice. It does not activate strongly on longer discursive sentences that discuss feelings or empathy descriptively, give other kinds of advice (boundaries, communication tactics, self-reflection), or narrate a situation rather than issuing a direct 'acknowledge/listen/validate X's feelings' instruction, even if empathy-related themes are present.

title: Self-care advice list items
description: This latent fires on short imperative bullet-point phrases recommending self-care, rest, or relaxation practices (e.g. 'Practice self-care', 'Take breaks', 'Practice mindfulness', 'Take deep breaths'), especially the initial header/label phrase of a listicle item before elaboration. It activates most strongly on the terse, formulaic naming of the practice itself (often bolded or followed by a colon), and less strongly but still noticeably on surrounding advice-giving sentences about prioritizing well-being, recharging, or managing stress. It does NOT activate strongly on longer explanatory or contextual sentences that discuss emotions, relationships, or general advice-giving without invoking one of these specific stock self-care/relaxation imperatives (e.g. sentences about setting boundaries, seeking therapy, or reflecting on motivations only weakly trigger it, and narrative or descriptive sentences unrelated to prescriptive self-care phrasing do not trigger it at all).

title: Sentence-initial 'This can/will help' construction
description: This latent fires on the specific syntactic pattern of a sentence beginning with the demonstrative 'This' followed by a modal verb ('can' or 'will') and often the word 'help', typically prefacing a benefit or positive outcome of a previously mentioned action or suggestion. It activates most strongly on short, templated openers like 'This can help', 'This will help you', 'This can help build confidence and motivation', regardless of what specific benefit follows. It also activates, though more weakly, on similar but slightly varied constructions elsewhere in advice text (e.g., 'This can help prevent misunderstandings', 'This shows...', 'This would have helped...') where the same lead-in structure appears mid-passage rather than as an isolated top hit. It does NOT activate on sentences that lack this specific 'This + modal (+help)' opening frame, such as advice sentences phrased with imperatives, conditionals, or other subjects (e.g., 'A professional can help you...', 'Focus on shared interests...', 'That's understandable'), even when they convey a similar advisory or benefit-stating function.

title: Suggesting compromise or mutual resolution
description: This latent fires on phrases that propose finding a compromise, middle ground, or mutually agreeable solution to a conflict, often phrased as a suggested question or directive ('Can we find a compromise?', 'Perhaps a compromise could be reached', 'Work together to find a solution that works for everyone'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic sentences that explicitly invoke words like 'compromise,' 'middle ground,' or 'solution that works for everyone/both parties,' typically appearing as advice or dialogue suggestions for resolving interpersonal disputes. It also activates, more weakly, on numbered list markers (e.g., '2.', '3.') that likely precede such compromise-oriented suggestions in structured advice text. It does NOT activate strongly on sentences that merely describe a conflict, give unilateral advice (e.g., setting boundaries, apologizing, seeking mediation from a third party), or discuss resolving a problem without framing it as a joint compromise/solution-seeking move.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and following period/asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated or numbered list, most strongly on '2.' but also on other digits like '3.', '4.', '5.' etc., often followed by bold markdown formatting for a list-item header. It activates specifically at the token position of the list-number marker itself, regardless of the content of the list (steps, tips, categories, solutions, etc.), and is largely agnostic to topic. It does not activate on the prose content of list items, bullet points marked with asterisks/dashes rather than numbers, or numbers appearing in non-list contexts such as measurements, dates, or arithmetic.

title: Advice to have an open, honest conversation
description: This latent fires on the stock advice-column formula 'Have an open and honest conversation with [person] about [topic]', typically issued as an imperative recommendation to a relationship-advice seeker, often as a bolded action-item header (e.g. 'Communicate openly**:'). It activates most strongly on the near-templatic phrase itself, regardless of which relationship (girlfriend, mom, boyfriend, sister, boss) or which concern (feelings, boundaries, concerns) fills the slots, and less strongly on looser paraphrases that still invoke the same 'talk openly/honestly' advice move (e.g. 'try to have an open and respectful conversation'). It does not activate on general discussion of communication as a topic, narrative descriptions of conversations that already happened, or other conflict-resolution advice (e.g. 'use I statements', 'choose the right time and place', 'set boundaries') that lacks the explicit 'open and honest conversation' recommendation phrasing.

title: Soliciting the listener's opinion
description: This latent activates most strongly on the exact phrase 'What do you think?' and more generally on brief conversational questions that invite the reader/listener to share their own opinion, feelings, or reaction (e.g. 'Do you agree or disagree?', 'How do you feel about it?', 'Is that correct?'). It fires on short, direct interrogatives placed at the end of an advice-giving or conversational turn, functioning as a rhetorical hand-off that prompts the other party to weigh in. It does not activate on statements that give advice, judgments, or conclusions themselves (e.g. 'NTA', 'you're not the asshole', 'I recommend...'), nor on declarative or open-ended narrative questions that ask for factual details rather than opinions (e.g. 'What kind of challenges is she facing?'); the strongest activation is reserved for the terse, generic opinion-soliciting question itself rather than elaborated or topic-specific questions.

title: Normalizing reassurance about imperfection and not being alone
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic reassurance statements that use universal quantifiers (nobody, everyone, no one, we all) or direct address (you're not alone) to normalize failure, mistakes, and imperfection, often as therapeutic clichés like 'Nobody is perfect, and it's okay to make mistakes' or 'You're not alone.' It activates most strongly on terse, template-like sentences combining a universalizing claim with a permission-granting clause ('it's okay to...'), frequently prefixed by 'Remember,' and peaks on the most repetitive, boilerplate versions of this comfort formula. It activates more weakly on longer, more elaborated or context-specific supportive advice (e.g., explaining why someone isn't to blame, validating a specific emotion, or giving concrete coping tips) that conveys similar emotional support but lacks the compact 'everyone/no one + it's okay' normalizing structure, and it does not activate on sentences that merely discuss mistakes or perfection factually without an interpersonal reassurance/comfort function.
